newsitem.title: ITALY: U.S. signals no grain subsidies against Argentina.
newsitem.headline: U.S. signals no grain subsidies against Argentina.

text.p: U.S. Agriculture secretary Dan Glickman and other U.S. officials indicated on Friday that Washington would not bring out its dormant wheat export subsidies to counter heavy price competition from Argentina.

Glickman told a news conference that while such a move would probably be legal, the United States had a traditional policy of only using the subsidies against countries which practiced government intervention in grain exports.
Argentina does not subsidise wheat exports.

"Obviously the Argentina siuation is worth watching," Glickman said, on being asked whether the U.S. would counter lower Argentine wheat prices with its Export Enhancement Program, designed to counter EU export subsidies but out of use for more than a year.

"I think it would be statutorily permissible to use (EEP) for market protection purposes, but we have made the policy judgement ... for an extensive period of time that it will not be used except to protect U.S. market share as a result of unfair trade or other government practices," he added.
Under Secretary of Agriculture Eugene Moos said prices would continue to fall if other exporters competed head-on with Argentina, which he expected to be competitive for a few months.

"All the recent bids in the world market were registered by the Argentines. They are having what is expected to be a bumper crop this year...in the neighbourhood of 10 million tonnes of wheat for export," Moos said.

"About half of that will go to Brazil and the rest will go to the world market at whatever price they can move it... This will have a depressing effect on world prices if the other exporting countries respond competitively to that action."
The United States, facing tight domestic wheat stocks, would not be a strong competitive force this year, he said.
U.S. officials travelling with Glickman at a Rome food summit said Washington was more concerned about EU export behaviour if EU prices fell below intervention storage prices.

While the EU appears to have satisified Washington that it is not aggressively subsidising wheat now, the officials said Washington would closely monitor whether Brussels decided to abandon its price link to U.S. wheat if internal prices fell.
If EU prices fall sharply, Brussels has the tough task of choosing between a possible flare-up with Washington by undercutting U.S. prices or paying for costly local storage.
Glickman said he was reassured by current EU actions but, once again, kept U.S. options open on the future of EEP.

"I will say again that while we have no present plans to use EEP, we don't rule out the ability to engage in those measures that we think will protect us from being unduly taken advantage of by other countries," he said.
